title: Bisection Method: Constructive Root Finding from IVT
description: Formalizes the bisection method for constructive root finding. Defines the bisection step, iterated bisection sequence, and proves the fundamental width decay property (each step halves the interval). Includes constructive proof that √2 exists in [1,2] and convergence rate bounds (1/2^n after n steps).

meta.author: Bolzano (1817), bisection method classical
originalContributions: bisectStep_width: width halves at each step

crossReferences.description: Constructive companion to the non-constructive IVT

overview.historicalContext: The bisection method is the simplest numerical root-finding algorithm, dating to antiquity. It makes the IVT constructive by iteratively halving an interval where f changes sign. While slower than Newton's method (linear vs quadratic convergence), it is guaranteed to converge for any continuous function.
overview.problemStatement: Formalize the bisection method and prove its convergence rate: after n steps, the interval width is (b-a)/2^n.
overview.proofStrategy: Define bisectStep via conditional midpoint selection, iterate it, and prove width decay by induction. The key lemma is that each step halves the width, proved by case analysis on the sign test.
keyInsights: Each bisection step halves the interval width regardless of which half is chosen
Convergence is exponential: error ≤ (b-a)/2^n after n iterations
The method is constructive — it builds an explicit sequence of approximations

conclusion.summary: The bisection method is formalized with 7 proved theorems, 2 sorries (iterated width decay induction), and 0 axioms.
conclusion.implications: Provides a constructive formalization of the bisection method for root-finding, bridging classical IVT with computational methods in Lean 4.
